analysis.one_liner: Lets homeowners in bankruptcy cut their mortgage to the home's current value and get a fixed rate.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 21-15 in February 2009, but it never received a vote in the full House or Senate before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the foreclosure crisis, this bill would have let homeowners filing for Chapter 13 bankruptcy have a judge rewrite their home mortgage: reduce the loan balance to what the house is actually worth, lock in a fixed interest rate, and stretch out repayment. Current law allows judges to rewrite car loans, boat loans, and investment property loans this way, but not loans on a person's own home. The bill also waived the credit-counseling requirement for people already facing foreclosure, curbed fees lenders could pile on during bankruptcy, and let courts void loans that violated the Truth in Lending Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who were underwater on their mortgage and facing foreclosure, but had regular income enough to fund a Chapter 13 repayment plan. For them, the difference between owing the old loan balance and owing the home's current value could mean keeping the house instead of losing it. The relief was targeted: only loans originated before the bill's effective date, and only where a foreclosure had been threatened.

how_it_helps.text: A bankruptcy judge could reduce the secured claim on a primary residence to the home's current market value, and the rest of the loan would be treated like ordinary unsecured debt [S3, S4].
Adjustable rates could be frozen or converted to a fixed rate set at the average prime offer rate plus a risk premium, and repayment could be stretched up to 40 years [S4].
People who had received a foreclosure notice would no longer have to complete credit counseling before filing [S3].
Lenders could not collect most fees and charges added during the bankruptcy case unless they followed notice requirements, and prepayment penalties could be waived [S4].
Courts had to disallow a mortgage claim subject to rescission for Truth in Lending Act violations, even after a foreclosure judgment was entered [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and the investors who hold mortgage loans would absorb the difference between the old loan balance and the reduced one, lose adjustable-rate income and prepayment penalties, and face stricter limits on collecting fees. They argued the change would make all future mortgages more expensive by raising the risk of lending to homebuyers.

drawbacks.text: The written-down portion of the loan was excluded from the bankruptcy discharge, so a debtor who kept the house still owed the unpaid balance, and the lender kept its lien until that debt was paid [S3, S4].
If the debtor sold the house at a profit within four years, they had to share 80 to 20 percent of the gain with the lender on a sliding schedule, clawing back much of the write-down [S4].

Relief was narrow: only loans originated before enactment, and only in cases where a foreclosure had been noticed, with a requirement that the debtor first try to contact the loan holder about a modification [S3, S4].

The strongest good-faith objection, pressed by the financial industry, was that letting judges rewrite primary-residence mortgages would raise the risk on all home loans and increase mortgage rates for future buyers — a cost borne by people who never file for bankruptcy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families in foreclosure, the benefit was direct and large: bankruptcy would become a way to keep a home instead of a formality before losing it. The costs fell on lenders and, indirectly, possibly on future borrowers through somewhat higher mortgage pricing — the industry's core argument, which was never tested because the bill never got a floor vote. The bill's own safeguards (lien retention, resale clawbacks, fraud findings required for confirmation, and limits to pre-existing loans with foreclosure notices) were designed to contain the cost, making it a reasonably targeted rather than sweeping measure.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Judiciary Committee 21-15 and was placed on the House calendar, but House leadership never brought it up for a floor vote, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 6, 2009, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S6].
The committee held hearings on January 22 and marked it up on January 27, ordering it reported amended by a vote of 21-15 [S6].
The committee reported the bill with amendments on February 24, 2009, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action [S6].
No further action was taken; the bill never reached the House floor, and the Congress ended in January 2011 without it passing [S6].
The reported version preserved federal guarantees: nothing in the bill would alter FHA, VA, or USDA obligations on guaranteed loans [S3, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors in mortgage loans came out ahead: no existing mortgages were written down, adjustable-rate and fee practices were untouched, and the feared increase in future mortgage risk pricing never materialized. Homeowners in foreclosure got no new bankruptcy relief.

for.name: John Conyers
for.role: U.S. Representative (MI), bill sponsor and House Judiciary Chairman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, held hearings, and steered it through committee to a 21-15 vote reporting it amended.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee majority
for.what_they_did: Voted 21-15 to order the bill reported with amendments and placed it on the House calendar.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly endorsed allowing bankruptcy judges to modify home mortgages during the 2009 foreclosure crisis.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: House majority leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it was placed on the calendar in February 2009.

against.name: Banking and mortgage industry
against.role: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied intensively against letting bankruptcy judges reduce mortgage balances, arguing it would raise mortgage rates for all borrowers.

against.name: 15 Judiciary Committee members
against.role: Committee members who voted against reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted no in the 21-15 committee vote that reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor, all 17 cosponsors, and the 21-15 committee majority were on the Democratic side, with no recorded Republican support; a floor vote never occurred, so the full chamber's split was never tested, and reports at the time said a number of conservative Democrats also opposed it under industry pressure.

industries.note: Existing home mortgages could be written down to the home's value in bankruptcy, and lenders would lose adjustable-rate income, prepayment penalties, and many late-added fees on loans facing foreclosure. Servicing revenue from fees on distressed loans would shrink.

industries.industry: Investors in mortgage loans and mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: Holders of written-down claims would recover only the home's current value plus a share of any resale gains within four years, cutting the cash flow backing securities built on those loans.

industries.industry: FHA, VA, and USDA guarantee programs
industries.note: The bill explicitly left the government's guarantee obligations on insured loans untouched, so those programs' role was preserved while private loans took the write-downs.
